dimensions.name: C-semantics, ABI & test-suite orientation

evidence.note: Read run_tests.py and utils.py, read filter.json, and counted tests per suite — established the test harness structure and scale before building.
Sampled concrete test cases from all three suites (c-testsuite, wacc, gcc-torture) and verified the toolchain (cargo/rustc/gcc/as/ld), i.e. the assembly/link path — matches the level-5 anchor.
Discovered and vendored the existing wrecc C-compiler crate; much of the ABI/assembly/semantic contract was inherited rather than independently researched, capping the independence of orientation.
Systematically read the reused compiler's type system, token model, parser and scanner to understand the target contract it was building on.
Repeatedly categorized failing tests by feature (casts, constants, doubles, alignment, page-boundary) — feature-level orientation shaping fixes.

Mined specific failing tests to infer exact semantics (divide-by-zero, ternary folding, array-size specifiers) and probed assembler alignment behavior — sustained level-8/10-flavored research, though reactive rather than anticipatory.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeded the level-5 anchor: beyond reading run_tests and sampling every suite, it continually mined failing tests to infer concrete semantic requirements and probed ABI/assembly edge cases like alignment and page boundaries (level-8/10 behaviors), sustained across the whole trajectory. It falls short of 8-10 because it vendored an existing compiler (wrecc) and inherited most of the ABI/codegen contract rather than deriving it from small reference cases, and its orientation was largely reactive fix-driven rather than an anticipatory, self-built taxonomy of the target contract. This places the observed behavior at a 7, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Feature staging & milestone structure

evidence.note: Up-front exploration of all three test suites, harness scripts, and toolchain establishes the problem space before any building — a foundation for staging, though no explicit milestone plan is authored here.

Rather than staging compiler passes from scratch, the agent adopted the existing wrecc crate as its base; the 'ordered hierarchy of passes' is largely inherited, so the agent's own decomposition is not a self-designed dependency-ordered pass plan.

After a full test run, the agent clustered failures into feature buckets (casts ch14, constants/doubles ch13, floats) and worked each bucket, re-running that specific subset as its done-check — feature milestones loosely tied to passing test subsets.

Continued the same pattern for short-circuit (ch4), page-boundary/alignment, ternary, and array-size features — each fix batch verified against its own test subset, but ordering is driven by what the full run surfaced rather than a deliberate dependency sequence.
Final full-suite runs and binary/status checks act as the terminal checkpoint; milestones remained failure-driven throughout with no re-prioritization by 'which features unlock most tests.'

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows a clear feature-level decomposition — failing tests grouped into feature clusters (casts, constants, floats, short-circuit, alignment, ternary, arrays), each verified against its own test subset — which is well beyond the vague 'lexer-then-parser' of anchor 3. But the pass hierarchy was inherited by adopting the wrecc crate rather than staged by the agent, and the milestone ordering is reactive/failure-driven rather than a deliberate dependency-aware sequence with explicit gating or smallest-viable-slice re-prioritization (anchor 8+). This matches anchor 5: clear pass structure plus a feature roadmap in reasonable order with milestones loosely tied to getting test subsets passing.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design

evidence.note: Read run_tests.py/utils.py/filter.json and sampled tests from all three suites before building — established how pass/fail is judged, the basis for a trustworthy verification loop.
Ran the full test suite at several checkpoints across the build, not just at the end — periodic global signal.
After fixes, ran targeted subsets grouped by suite (wacc chapters, c-testsuite numbers, gcc-torture names) and re-checked the specific previously-failing tests — subset runs driving fixes.
Reduced failures to individual test files, compiling each with ccc to /tmp and running — per-test reproduction rather than only full-suite.
Built python helpers (PYTHONPATH=/app) to reproduce the harness's per-test flags/expected output — verification infra slightly beyond what was handed over.
Localized specific failing tests to the responsible compiler pass by reading fold.rs, typechecker, codegen, scanner — root-cause isolation distinguishing lexer/parser/sema/codegen defects.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a genuine test-driven loop: periodic full-suite runs, categorized subset runs by suite after each fix, per-test reproductions, custom harness-reproducing helpers, and defect localization to specific compiler passes — well above anchor 5. It stops short of anchor 8 because it never inspects generated assembly or diffs against known-correct output, relying on exit-code/program-output signal, and shows no regression-guard scripting. That places it at a 7, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Pass-rate tracking & thrash detection

evidence.note: Runs the full run_tests.sh suite repeatedly across the whole trajectory, giving recurring whole-suite pass counts rather than a single early check.
Pulls failing tests organized by suite/category (wacc chapters, c-testsuite numbers, gcc-torture names), showing a done-vs-remaining picture segmented by category.
Re-runs specific previously-failing tests after fixes to confirm progress and catch breakage — running verification tied to a feature tally.
Repeated build/test cycles on a single gcc-torture test (20000314-2) — some circular debugging on one case, though eventually bounded and returned to full-suite run at 116.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent keeps a running tally via recurring full-suite runs interleaved with category-segmented targeted retesting (steps 122-125, 139-141, 163-165), and re-verifies after fixes — matching the level-5 anchor. It reaches toward 8 by organizing remaining work by category, but falls short of 8-10: it shows a stretch of looping on one stubborn test (96-114) and no visible structured live scoreboard or explicit regression attribution. Net behavior sits at 5.

dimensions.name: Design revision under falsified assumptions

evidence.note: Agent adopted the existing wrecc compiler (already typed HIR/MIR/LIR) and copied it into /app/compiler. This inherited a sound architecture, so the agent never confronted a falsified design of its own — limiting the scope for genuine design revision on this dimension.

Repeated localized patching of the same number/float scanning subsystem across multiple rounds, iterating with local fixes + rebuild + retest rather than restructuring — closer to symptom-level patching (anchor 3).

Feature-gap fixes (constant folding, ternary, return-path check, array-size specifier, global alignment) each added locally to the existing architecture and re-verified with targeted test subsets — reworking affected components and re-verifying (toward anchor 5), but never a structural refactor.

Codegen/typechecker/LIR were pre-existing, well-typed passes from wrecc; the agent read them and made point edits, confirming no architectural revision was undertaken by the agent itself (no anchor-8 refactor).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent adopted an existing, well-architected compiler (wrecc) with type info already threaded through its IR, so it never had to revise a broken design of its own — the central challenge this dimension probes. Its observed adaptation consists entirely of localized feature/symptom patches, with repeated iteration on the same scanner subsystem, each followed by rebuild and re-verification. This sits between anchor 3 (local symptom patching, resisting structural change) and anchor 5 (reworks affected component and re-verifies), with no evidence of recognizing an architectural limitation and executing a deliberate refactor (anchor 8) — hence a 4.

dimensions.name: Compiler architecture & IR foresight

evidence.note: Agent comparatively evaluated existing Rust C compilers (chibicc, wrecc, wrecc_compiler) via cargo, reading main.rs/Cargo.toml/README and module layout — architecture due-diligence, but on someone else's design rather than authoring its own pass boundaries.

Copied the entire wrecc_compiler-0.2.0 source tree and include dir into /app/compiler. The typed AST/IR, symbol tables, HIR/MIR/LIR passes and type/layout model were adopted wholesale, not designed by the agent.

Agent read the inherited core representations (types.rs, token.rs, parser, scanner, typechecker, HIR decl.rs, codegen) confirming the design already anticipates types/structs/casts before extending it — comprehension of an already-extensible architecture.

All later hard-feature work (casts, ternary codegen, array-size const-eval, .align/.data emission, float folding) landed as additive patches into existing passes with no wholesale rewrites — evidence the architecture accommodates the full contract, though the accommodating design was inherited.

dimensions.reasoning: The architecture actually driving the deliverable is strongly separated with a typed IR (HIR/MIR/LIR), symbol/scope tables and a type/layout model into which advanced features slot additively — behavior consistent with the level-8 anchor. However, this foresight was inherited by vendoring the mature wrecc compiler, not authored by the agent; the agent's own architecture meta-work was limited to selecting a base that could support the contract, verifying it by reading its core structures, and applying additive patches. Because the observed clean separation and additive feature-landing are real (well above the level-5 'adequate for early milestones') yet the design judgment was borrowed rather than demonstrated, I place it at 6.

rubric.task_read: This is an extreme long-horizon build: a from-scratch C compiler in Rust spanning lexer, full preprocessor, parser, semantic analysis, and x86-64 codegen, plus many advanced features (structs/unions, switch/case, typedef/casts, globals, short-circuit eval), gated by 780 tests across three real-world suites that must all pass. Difficulty comes from sheer scope, deep interdependence between passes, an implicit contract (C semantics + x86-64 ABI) the agent must recover, and the near-certainty that naive early design decisions will break under later features. A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in every meta-work faculty — deep orientation, staged milestones tied to test subsets, relentless test-driven verification, accurate pass-rate tracking, and willingness to refactor architecture mid-flight.

dimensions.name: C-semantics, ABI & test-suite orientation
dimensions.description: Understanding C language semantics, the x86-64 System V ABI/assembly conventions, and the structure/content of the three test suites before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 'spec' is largely implicit — correct behavior is defined by C semantics, the calling convention, and what the 780 tests actually exercise. Acting without recovering this contract guarantees rework across nearly every pass.

anchors.0: Starts emitting code with no inspection of the test suites, run_tests.sh, or ABI conventions; guesses at behavior.
anchors.3: Skims run_tests.sh and writes a trivial hello-world compile; no systematic look at what features the tests demand or how the ABI/relocation works.
anchors.5: Reads run_tests.sh, samples tests from each suite, and establishes the basic x86-64 calling convention and assembly emission path before building core codegen.
anchors.8: Systematically categorizes tests by feature/difficulty, extracts the concrete language subset required, and probes ABI edge cases (struct passing, sizes/alignment, relocations) by compiling small reference cases; orientation directly shapes the build order.
anchors.10: Sustained, iterative research: continually mines failing tests to infer exact semantic requirements (integer promotion, evaluation order, layout rules), verifies assumptions against the assembler/linker behavior, and maintains a living understanding of the target contract that anticipates features before they are reached.

dimensions.name: Feature staging & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the compiler into an ordered hierarchy of passes and feature milestones, each with an explicit done-check (e.g. a passing test subset).
dimensions.why_it_matters: You cannot build all of C at once; the difference between steady progress and thrashing is a sane dependency-ordered plan (expressions before control flow before types before structs) with checkpoints.

anchors.0: No decomposition; attempts the whole compiler as one undifferentiated push or jumps between unrelated features at random.
anchors.3: Vague ordering ('do lexer, then parser, then codegen') with no feature-level milestones or explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Clear pass structure plus a feature roadmap in a reasonable dependency order, with milestones loosely tied to getting some tests passing.
anchors.8: Fine-grained, dependency-aware milestones each bound to a concrete test subset as its done-signal, sequenced so each milestone builds on verified prior ones; ordering reflects which features unlock the most tests.
anchors.10: A living milestone hierarchy that is re-prioritized as data arrives — smallest-viable-slice ordering, explicit gating criteria per milestone, and deliberate deferral of hard/rare features until foundations are proven, sustained coherently across the whole horizon.

dimensions.name: Test-driven verification design
dimensions.description: Deliberately building/using checks — incremental runs of test subsets, minimal repro cases, diffing against expected behavior — rather than assuming generated code is correct.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With 780 opaque pass/fail tests and a compiler where any pass can silently miscompile, a disciplined verification loop is the only way to know progress is real and to localize defects.

anchors.0: Never runs the tests until the very end, or writes code with no way to confirm correctness; assumes success.
anchors.3: Runs the full suite occasionally as the only check; no isolation of failures, no smaller probes.
anchors.5: Runs relevant test subsets after each feature and uses the pass/fail signal to guide fixes.
anchors.8: Builds a tight loop: reduces failing tests to minimal reproductions, inspects generated assembly, and compares against known-correct output to pinpoint which pass is wrong before editing.
anchors.10: Engineers verification infrastructure beyond what's handed over — categorized/scriptable subset runs, regression guards so fixed tests stay fixed, and root-cause isolation that distinguishes lexer/parser/sema/codegen defects — sustaining fast, trustworthy signal across the entire build.

dimensions.name: Pass-rate tracking & thrash detection
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture (which tests/features pass), and detecting regressions, circular debugging, or stalls across a very long horizon.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Over hundreds of features and edits, it is easy to lose the plot, regress previously-passing tests, or loop on one stubborn failure; an accurate live picture is what sustains net forward motion.

anchors.0: No sense of how many tests pass or which features remain; edits blindly with no scoreboard.
anchors.3: Occasional whole-suite counts but no tracking of trends, regressions, or which categories are outstanding.
anchors.5: Keeps a running tally of pass counts by suite/feature and notices when a change breaks previously-passing tests.
anchors.8: Maintains a structured, current view of pass rate by category and remaining work, and recognizes when stuck on one test — bounding effort and moving on rather than looping.
anchors.10: Treats pass-rate as a managed signal: detects regressions immediately and attributes them, spots circular/thrashing debugging early and deliberately changes tactics, and continuously re-derives the highest-leverage remaining work from the scoreboard.

dimensions.name: Design revision under falsified assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising architecture, data structures, or approach when a later feature (types, structs, ABI detail) exposes that an earlier design cannot support it.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Compilers are notorious for early choices (untyped AST, ad-hoc register allocation, string-based codegen) that collapse under types/structs; the ability to recognize and refactor rather than pile hacks decides whether the tail of the task is reachable.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on a broken design, piling special-cases and hacks even as failures compound.
anchors.3: Patches symptoms locally; resists structural change even when the same class of bug keeps recurring.
anchors.5: When an approach clearly fails, reworks the affected component and re-verifies rather than forcing it.
anchors.8: Recognizes when a limitation is architectural (not local), makes a deliberate refactor (e.g. adding type info through the AST/IR), and confirms the change unblocks the stuck feature class.
anchors.10: Proactively detects design strain before it becomes a wall, weighs refactor-vs-workaround explicitly, executes larger restructurings cleanly while protecting already-passing tests, and updates the plan/design record so the correction propagates instead of recurring.

dimensions.name: Compiler architecture & IR foresight
dimensions.description: Choosing pass boundaries and core data structures (AST/IR, symbol tables, type representation) with enough foresight to accommodate the full required feature set rather than painting into a corner.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike generic decomposition (what to do when) or adaptation (fixing after breakage), this is the upfront design judgment specific to compilers: a representation that anticipates types, structs, and the ABI avoids the most expensive class of rework on this task.

anchors.0: No deliberate architecture; monolithic, ad-hoc string-munging with no separable passes or reusable structures.
anchors.3: Minimal structure that works for the first trivial cases but has no provision for types, scopes, or layout.
anchors.5: Clean separation of lexer/parser/sema/codegen with data structures adequate for the early feature milestones.
anchors.8: Core representations (typed AST/IR, symbol/scope tables, type/layout model) are designed with the later hard features in mind, so structs/typedef/switch slot in without wholesale rewrites.
anchors.10: Architecture demonstrably anticipates the full contract — extensible IR and type system, clear invariants between passes — enabling most advanced features to be added additively; foresight is evidenced by later features landing cleanly rather than by luck.
